title: Chitralekha Comes for Aniruddha
story:
She came to Dwaraka with a theft on her mind and a name on her lips: Aniruddha.

Chitralekha made her way to the city and settled near the palace of Vasudeva, turning over the question of how she might find Pradyumna's son and carry him away. While she sat thinking, she saw the ascetic Narada meditating in the water. Her eyes widened with joy. She approached him, saluted him, and stood before him with her head bowed. Narada blessed her, and then asked, gently, what she had come for.

With folded hands she told him everything. She was a messenger, she said, come to take Aniruddha with her. In the city of Sonitpura lived the great asura Bana, and Bana had a daughter, Usha, the most beautiful of maidens. By the boon of a goddess, Usha had chosen Aniruddha as her husband — a man she had never met except in a dream. The dream had claimed her utterly, and Chitralekha meant to take him to her. But after she had carried Aniruddha to Sonitpura, Krishna must learn the truth, for a great encounter would follow: Bana was too powerful for Aniruddha to defeat, yet the large-armed Krishna would vanquish the thousand-armed asura. And that was what she feared. Krishna, when angered, could consume even the three worlds with a curse; she begged Narada to arrange matters so that Usha might have her husband and she herself might not be burned by that wrath.

Narada gave his answer. “I offer you protection,” he said. “Shorn of fear, hear what I say. If any encounter takes place while you steal away Aniruddha to the apartments of the maidens, remember me — I am fond of seeing battles, and take great pleasure in them. And accept the Tamasika learning, which I have mastered by hard austerities, that can infatuate all the worlds.”

“So be it,” said Chitralekha. She saluted the sage, and set out through the sky, searching for Aniruddha's house.

She found it in the centre of Dwaraka: the palace of Kama, the god of love, and beside it the palace where Aniruddha lived — golden altars, pillars of gold and sapphire, garlands hanging along the walls, jars of cool water set at the doors, peacocks carved on the turrets, and rows of celestial buildings set with jewels and coral, filled with the music of the Gandharvas. And there she saw Aniruddha, playing in the midst of the most beautiful women of the court as the moon shines among the stars. Hundreds of women attended on him. Seated like Kubera on a fine seat, he was drinking Madhvika wine; sweet songs rose and fell in time; accomplished dancers moved before him. But Chitralekha saw no pleasure in him. His mind was not on the wine; he showed dislike even for drinking. She watched, and understood: surely his mind is busy with the dream. And her anxiety fell away.

Hiding herself in the sky above the palace, she spoke to him in sweet words, asking whether all was well with him, and then delivered her message. “I have come to you from Usha,” she said, “the maiden whom you saw in a dream and married, and who cherishes you at her heart. She is weeping, and yawning, and sighing, for she cannot see you. She will live if you go to her; forsooth, in your absence she will die.”

The words found their mark. By the power of her Tamasika illusion Chitralekha overpowered everyone in the palace except the prince himself, and carried Aniruddha away through the sky to Sonitpura — to a maiden's rooms where Usha was waiting for the man of her dream.
reflection: The whole errand runs on illusion — the dream that joined Usha to a man she had never met, the Tamasika learning that lets Chitralekha move unseen through a city — yet every deception serves a genuine longing. Narada's blessing is characteristic: he helps gladly, and asks only to be remembered when the fighting begins.
next_story_tease: But Vana's city would not keep its secret long, and the thousand-armed king had soldiers enough to answer it.
hero_scene: Chitralekha, hidden in the sky above Aniruddha's jewelled palace in Dwaraka, speaking down to the prince as he sits among dancers and musicians, his mind elsewhere — the moon among stars, and the messenger who moves like thought.
visual_elements: Chitralekha concealed in the sky above the palace
Aniruddha seated like Kubera among hundreds of beautiful women, drinking wine he does not want
the palace with golden altars, sapphire pillars, peacocks on the turrets, jars of water and garlands
the Gandharva music filling the air
